Zoom through space and time

A telescope receives light that has travelled from an earlier scene. The violet chronal echo is A.R.G.O.'s science-fiction addition: an imagined information path that lets the crew explore a much older scene while the ship stays home.

In this simple model, distance in light-years is also ordinary light's travel time in years.
The onboard clock keeps moving forward normally.

Two ways to make a view

Ordinary light: event → telescope, future-directedChronal echo: fictional information map

Ordinary signal:   Δtlight = D/c   ·   Fictional scan:   q(τ) = q0 − ΔT τ/TA

For your settings, ordinary light needs 2,500 years. The story's echo would have to map 2,500 years of remote history into 5 minutes aboard A.R.G.O. That is a continuous viewing schedule, not a solved engine.

What the rate means

The remote scene-address changes by about 2.63 × 10⁸ remote seconds for each second of crew time. The ratio can be huge because this imagined channel connects events that ordinary light would take thousands of years to link. It is not a claim that a photon locally travels at that speed.

Science-fiction rule: the crew's body and clock stay with A.R.G.O. The chronal echo carries a changing information pattern; the dome and a fictional neural display turn it into a lived view. Quantum entanglement may help label or compare patterns, but known entanglement cannot send the picture or choose the past scene. The story's echo supplies that missing rule.

To make the imagined channel more than a pretty line, a future theory must specify its field equation, energy and momentum source, noise and resolution, endpoint events, and causal rules. If it lets information reach the past, it must also explain how the resulting history remains self-consistent. Every point on the plotted line is a demand on that theory.

Teaching illustration. The straight violet line visualizes the requested continuous map; it is not a computed solution of Einstein's equations or quantum field theory.
